source.title: Neuralyzing the Trace: Selective Representation-Level Unlearning with Contrastive Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Itai Zehavi; Fanny Jourdan; Ulrich Aivodji

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Figures are referred to and captioned, but their plotted values are not available in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates representation-level unlearning and explicitly qualifies what it establishes: SCALPEL is an inference-time filter, not deletion of the parametric trace. It does not test the specified recovery attacks.
record.gate_note: The paper reports an unlearning benchmark and a paraphrase-based evaluation, but the plotted outcomes are not available as readable values here. Its discussion of recovery through paraphrases, relearning, and other prompts cites prior work; those cited results are not rows. It does not test relearning attacks, activation-direction ablation as a recovery attack, quantization, jailbreaks, or a counter-method's resistance to those attacks.
record.test_reason: This is a method paper. It proposes SCALPEL, an inference-time contrastive-SAE filter, and reports its forget/utility trade-offs on TOFU against NMF, SAE, GradDiff and RMU. It runs no recovery attack: no relearning, direction ablation, quantization, or reported jailbreak/paraphrase result. Its remark that SCALPEL does not erase the parametric trace describes how the method is built. It is not an analysis showing that an unlearning method blocks access rather than deleting. The shallow-unlearning finding (Hong et al., Yuan et al.) is cited only as motivation.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. SCALPEL improves over NMF and standard-SAE interventions and is competitive with RMU and GradDiff on TOFU across three small models. The authors stress it is an inference-time filter, not certified deletion, and that the trace may resurface if the filter is disabled or bypassed.
record.recipe_differences: SCALPEL is a contrastive sparse-autoencoder representation-level intervention that subtracts selected decoded feature contributions at inference. It is not a recovery-attack recipe and does not test the listed attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: The benchmark sweeps intervention strength. The paper also notes that results may depend on the intervention layer, SAE architecture and latent dimension, contrastive settings, augmentation, feature-selection threshold, and feature geometry; it does not report a systematic layer-selection study.
record.problems: Recovery attacks central to the claim are not run. The supplied text does not include readable plotted values for the benchmark or paraphrase-based evaluation, and the authors acknowledge that their perturbation bound concerns representation-space magnitude rather than downstream behavior.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for baseline methods: the supplied text gives qualitative comparisons, while the benchmark curves' readable per-method values are unavailable. The paraphrase-based evaluation is listed as a metric but has no extractable outcome in the supplied text.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover forgotten knowledge; near-chance accuracy is not shown in readable values.
All parts; no ablation or bypass of the filter, and no trace analysis of RMU or GradDiff.
Paraphrase-based evaluation is listed as a metric but no result is reported in text; no jailbreak, cross-language or in-context attack is run.
SCALPEL is not claimed or tested to resist recovery attacks.

missing.what: The paraphrase-based evaluation listed among the metrics. If it appears in the multi-metric figures, it may bear on recovery by rephrasing, but no values are readable.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's tests/T5 classification and its C 'supports' label should be dropped. The paper's statements about hiding versus deletion are caveats about its own method's design or are cited from prior work. Table 3 margins are selection values and should not be rows.

versions.untested_parts: The benchmark measures forgetting and retained utility, but does not test whether simple attacks recover the knowledge. The supplied text does not provide readable values establishing that targeted accuracy reaches near chance.
No recovery fine-tuning or other small-set relearning attack is performed.
The paper states that SCALPEL does not erase the parametric trace and uses an internal filter, but does not test whether removing or ablating that filter restores the knowledge.

A paraphrase-based evaluation is listed among the metrics, but the supplied text gives no readable result for it. No separate jailbreak, other-language recovery, or in-context-information attack result is stated.
The paper does not test whether SCALPEL or another method resists the specified recovery attacks.

rows.measure: Whether the intervention deletes the parametric trace or filters its expression
rows.value: Authors state SCALPEL does not erase the parametric trace and instead applies a persistent internal filter when selected features activate.
rows.note: This is the authors' stated scope of the method, not a direct experiment disabling or bypassing the filter.
rows.check: This is not a result. It is the authors' description of their own method's design (an inference-time filter that leaves weights unchanged). It is not evidence that an unlearning method hides knowledge it appears to delete, and nothing was disabled or bypassed to test recovery.
